definitions.definition: Exchange of data between two devices through a transmission medium, via a system made of hardware and software.
Unidirectional communication in which the entire channel capacity carries data in one direction only, e.g. keyboard to monitor.
Both stations transmit and receive simultaneously, with the capacity of the link shared between the two directions.
Every device has a dedicated point-to-point link to every other device; a network of n nodes needs n(n−1)/2 links.
A usually privately owned network linking devices in a single office, building or campus, e.g. Ethernet or WiFi.
Network providing long-distance transmission over large geographic areas; it connects hosts through a communication subnet.
Two insulated copper wires twisted together in a helix; carrying the signal as a voltage difference gives immunity to noise.
Transmission system using light pulses through an ultra-thin glass fiber; presence of light denotes a 1 bit, absence a 0.
Seven-layer framework for understanding and designing how network functions are partitioned and communicate.
An escape byte is inserted before every accidental flag byte in the data so the flag can still serve as frame delimiter.
A 0 bit is stuffed after five consecutive 1s in the data so the flag pattern 01111110 never occurs inside a frame.
Complement of the sum of data words sent with a message; receiver's sum of the whole codeword being 0 means no error.
Polynomial error-detecting code; the remainder of modulo-2 division of the augmented dataword by a generator is appended.
Sender transmits one frame and waits for its acknowledgement before sending the next; sequence numbers are modulo 2.
Sender retransmits all unacknowledged frames starting from the damaged or lost one; receive window size is 1.
Only the damaged or timed-out frame is retransmitted and buffered frames are delivered in order; window size ≤ 2^m/2.
Technique of temporarily delaying an outgoing acknowledgement so it can be attached to the next outgoing data frame.
Bit-oriented protocol for point-to-point and multipoint links, using I, S and U frames.
Point-to-Point Protocol: byte-oriented framing with LCP for link setup, authentication protocols and NCPs for network layer data.
Earliest random-access method: each station sends whenever it has a frame; vulnerable time 2×Tfr, max throughput 0.184.
Stations may transmit only at the start of a time slot; vulnerable time halves to Tfr and max throughput rises to 0.368.
Carrier sense multiple access with collision detection; frame transmission time must be at least twice the propagation time.
Collision-avoidance access method for wireless networks using interframe space, contention window and acknowledgements.
Stations outside each other's hearing range collide at the receiver; solved with RTS/CTS handshake frames.
Timer set by stations hearing an RTS frame, showing how long they must wait before sensing the channel (virtual sensing).
Data-link device that connects LANs and separates collision domains, forwarding only frames addressed across it.
Router stores a fully arrived packet, verifies its checksum, then forwards it to the next router toward the destination.
Routing technique in which every incoming packet is sent out on every outgoing line except the one it arrived on.
Bellman-Ford routing: each node keeps a vector of least costs to every node and shares it with immediate neighbours.
Routers keep raising the cost of a lost route toward infinity using stale second-hand updates after a link failure.
Stabilization technique: a node does not advertise a route back to the neighbour from which it learned that route.
Each node floods packets describing its local connections, learns the full topology and computes its forwarding table using Dijkstra's algorithm.
Broadcast rule: a packet is forwarded only if it arrived on the link normally used to send packets toward its source.
Encapsulating a packet of one protocol inside the payload of an intervening network's packets to reach a same-type network.
32-bit address uniquely defining a device's connection to the Internet, written in dotted-decimal notation.
Dividing a single large network into multiple smaller networks; it increases the number of 1s in the mask.
Combining several class C blocks into one larger supernetwork; it decreases the number of 1s in the mask.
Maps private internal addresses to a company's public IP using the TCP source port as table index.
Server service that leases IP addresses and configures host parameters automatically for clients joining a network.
Control packet sent back to the source host by a congested router, ordering it to reduce its traffic.
Traffic shaper that turns bursty traffic into a fixed-rate outflow; packets wait in a FIFO queue drained at a constant rate.
Idle hosts accumulate tokens as credit for later bursts; one token is consumed for every unit of data sent.
Connectionless, unreliable transport protocol adding only port addresses, checksum and length to the services of IP.
Connection-oriented, reliable transport protocol delivering byte streams in order with flow and congestion control.
TCP connection establishment: client sends SYN, server answers SYN+ACK, and client confirms with a final ACK segment.
Internet service that maps host names to IP addresses and back using a distributed hierarchy of name servers.
Protocol defining the MTA client and server commands and responses used to move e-mail between systems.
Transforms non-ASCII e-mail data to NVT ASCII data for transmission through the Internet.
Copies files between hosts using two TCP connections: control on port 21 and data on port 20.
Hypertext Transfer Protocol used mainly to access data on the WWW; a client request message gets a server response message.
